source.title: LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
source.authors: Ahmadreza Jeddi; Marco Ciccone; B. Taati

page_placements.theme: Weight sharing, recurrence and parallel streams add computation beyond stored parameters

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether downstream benchmark performance changes with additional inference compute in looped language models, but does not fit or test the original parameter/token/training-compute scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws and uses a token budget described as following Chinchilla scaling, but does not measure power-law exponents, extrapolate larger runs from smaller ones, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own results do test downstream accuracy across loop budgets (V6). Perplexity across inference budgets is recorded as a related finding, not as a test of training-compute scaling.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper on depth-elastic looped Transformers. It cites Chinchilla only to set a ~25B-token training budget. Its results compare LoopFormer with baselines across inference loop budgets. It fits no power law over parameters, tokens or training compute, and does no extrapolation or allocation search. The loop-count gains are its own method's performance under test-time compute, not downstream predictability from model or training scale (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that shortcut-consistency training lets one looped model work across user-chosen loop budgets. Shorter budgets stay informative and more loops smoothly improve perplexity and reasoning, avoiding the collapse seen with early exiting. They make no claim about training scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: Uses shortcut-modulated looped Transformers and evaluates variable inference loop budgets, rather than fitting loss scaling laws or finding a training-compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.method_sensitivity: Inference budget and trajectory schedule affect outcomes; the authors report that schedule choice causes a spread of approximately 1.4 perplexity and approximately 1.3 accuracy points for the (3 ⊗ 8), M = 4 study, with a perplexity spread nearly 3 for (2 ⊗ 12), M = 6.

fits_no_version.finding: For LoopFormer (3⊗k), perplexity falls and average zero-shot accuracy rises as inference loops increase from 2 to 4 to 8. On Pile, perplexity goes 14.3→11.12→10.28; accuracy goes 40.36→43.73→44.81.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In budget-conditioned looped LMs, more inference loops (test-time depth) lower perplexity and raise downstream accuracy smoothly.

record.problems: The evidence concerns looped models trained on approximately ∼25B tokens, with a small set of configurations and inference budgets; it does not fit scaling laws or test extrapolation. The reported trajectory-schedule comparisons show that schedule choice can substantially affect outcomes. The text reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: Other models, loop budgets, benchmark task-specific accuracy values, and results in Table 1 are not separately extracted; the selected Appendix B.2 Table 2 rows report the main LoopFormer budget trend, while the main-table results substantially overlap. Figure-only results are also omitted.

untested.parts: No sweep or power-law fit over parameters, tokens or training compute.
No compute-optimal allocation search; the Chinchilla token budget is assumed.
Varies blocks k and loops, but not shape at fixed parameter count with untied weights.
Text only; no other modality or regime.
No downstream-versus-scale or versus-pretraining-loss relation is fitted or tested.

record.verdict_notes: Non-looped baselines at 6, 12 and 24 layers (Table 1) show perplexity 11.13/9.98/9.49 and accuracy 42.73/44.93/45.27. This is only a 4x range of baseline models, not a scaling study, so it is not recorded as a test. Training tokens (~25B) were set 'in accordance with Chinchilla scaling', so the study uses that result as a tool.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or sweeps over parameter count, training tokens, or training compute.
No prediction of larger-run loss from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-training-compute search for an optimal parameter/token allocation.
The study varies loop count and block depth, but does not compare depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count to test whether architecture details change loss only slightly.
Only text language modeling and reasoning are studied; no other modality or the listed alternative training regimes are tested.
Tests downstream accuracy across inference loop budgets, but does not establish a predictive function from scale or pretraining loss, nor test a broad range of model sizes or training scales.
No scaling-law exponent or compute-optimal allocation is fitted or compared across fitting choices.

relation.reason: The study applies a scaling-law finding to its training setup but reports inference-loop performance, without fitting training scaling laws, testing extrapolation, or estimating compute-optimal allocations.

tranche.reason: Section 4 uses Chinchilla scaling to select a 25B-token training budget; the reported experiments evaluate the authors' elastic-depth method rather than testing a catalog claim version.

source_check.notes: R1–R12 report the study's own method performance across inference budgets; they are not evidence for the listed training-scaling claim versions. The authors' conclusion about elastic inference and reduced representational stagnation is accurately paraphrased.

reader_labels.reason: Average downstream zero-shot accuracy rises from 40.36 to 43.73 to 44.81 as budget increases (R4, R8, R12); this supports improvement in the tested looped-model setting, but not a predictive law.
